---
title: "Mapping a change"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5.2, dpi = 100,
  fig.retina = 2, dev = "ragg_png", out.width = "100%"
)
options(gglaplot2.font = "inter")
library(ggplot2)
library(gglaplot2)
set.seed(7)
b <- gla_boroughs
b$change <- round(runif(nrow(b), -5, 2), 1)
```

A map of a change is the most asked-about chart in this package, so this
page walks through one from the first draft to the version that goes out,
with what each argument does and the mistakes that come up. The
[Maps](maps.html) page has the other map types.

The data is a change by borough: a column that runs below and above zero,
here a percentage change from minus five to plus two. A change wants a
diverging scale because zero means something, a fall against a rise, and
the colour should say which side of it an area sits on.

```{r data}
head(b[, c("name", "change")])
range(b$change)
```

## The first draft

Three layers: the boroughs filled by the change, the diverging stepped
scale, and the map theme.

```{r first}
ggplot(b) +
  geom_gla_sf(aes(fill = change)) +
  scale_fill_gla_b("diverging", name = NULL) +
  theme_gla_map()
```

`scale_fill_gla_b("diverging")` did four things without being asked:

- Zero is a cut. Nothing straddles it, so every area is plainly a fall or a
  rise.
- The step is one size on both sides, taken from the range of the data the
  way ggplot2 picks axis breaks, and counted out from zero until the data
  is covered. Here the falls run to minus five and the rises to two, so
  there are more steps below zero than above.
- Each side is coloured from one ramp, red below and blue above, so the
  first step below zero is as deep a red as the first step above is a blue.
  A side with fewer steps stops at a lighter colour; it is not stretched to
  the darkest.
- The legend stands on the right, reading top to bottom, whichever theme
  the chart uses.

`name = NULL` drops the legend title, since the subtitle will say what the
values are.

## Fixing the number of steps

The draft gave three steps below and one above because that is what the
data needed. When the chart is one of a set, or the data will be refreshed,
set `steps` and the count holds whatever the numbers do.

```{r steps}
ggplot(b) +
  geom_gla_sf(aes(fill = change)) +
  scale_fill_gla_b("diverging", name = NULL, steps = 3) +
  theme_gla_map()
```

Each side now has three bins at its own step width: two wide for the falls,
one wide for the rises, each rounded up to a sensible number so the legend
reads cleanly. `steps = c(2, 4)` is two below and four above.

```{r steps-uneven}
ggplot(b) +
  geom_gla_sf(aes(fill = change)) +
  scale_fill_gla_b("diverging", name = NULL, steps = c(2, 4)) +
  theme_gla_map()
```

## Setting the cuts yourself

For full control, give `breaks` and `limits`. The breaks are the cuts and
the limits are the two ends, so three bins a side is the lower limit plus
two cuts below zero, zero itself, two cuts above zero and the upper limit.
This is what `steps = 3` worked out for the data above, written by hand.

```{r by-hand}
ggplot(b) +
  geom_gla_sf(aes(fill = change)) +
  scale_fill_gla_b("diverging", name = NULL, limits = c(-6, 3),
                   breaks = c(-4, -2, 0, 1, 2)) +
  theme_gla_map()
```

Hand-set breaks stay where they are when the data changes, which is the
point of them and the catch: a refresh that moves outside the limits is
clipped, as the next section shows. `steps` with `limits` is the middle
way, dividing the limits you set into the count you want.

## An area far from the rest

One borough that has fallen much further than the others takes the detail
from everything else, since the steps have to reach it.

```{r outlier}
b$lopsided <- b$change
b$lopsided[b$name == "Tower Hamlets"] <- -38
ggplot(b) +
  geom_gla_sf(aes(fill = lopsided)) +
  scale_fill_gla_b("diverging", name = NULL) +
  theme_gla_map()
```

Set `limits` to the range that shows the rest, and the outlier takes the
end step. The chart has to say so, which is what `note` is for.

```{r outlier-held}
ggplot(b) +
  geom_gla_sf(aes(fill = lopsided)) +
  scale_fill_gla_b("diverging", name = NULL, limits = c(-6, 3), steps = 3) +
  gla_labs(
    title = "One borough has fallen far",
    subtitle = "Percentage change, synthetic data",
    note = "Tower Hamlets, at -38, is shown in the lowest step"
  ) +
  theme_gla_map()
```

## When the dividing line is not zero

`midpoint` moves the neutral and the counting. An index against a base of
100, or a change against the London average, reads the same way with the
midpoint there.

```{r midpoint}
b$index <- round(100 + b$change * 3, 1)
ggplot(b) +
  geom_gla_sf(aes(fill = index)) +
  scale_fill_gla_b("diverging", name = NULL, midpoint = 100, steps = 2) +
  gla_labs(title = "An index against 100", subtitle = "Synthetic data") +
  theme_gla_map()
```

## Labels on the legend

The legend takes a `labels` function like any ggplot2 scale. The data here
is already in percentage points, so `label_gla_percent(scale = 1)` adds the
sign without multiplying; data held as fractions, where 0.05 is five per
cent, takes `label_gla_percent()` as it is.

```{r labels}
ggplot(b) +
  geom_gla_sf(aes(fill = change)) +
  scale_fill_gla_b("diverging", name = NULL, steps = 3,
                   labels = label_gla_percent(scale = 1)) +
  theme_gla_map()
```

## The finished chart

The title states the finding, the subtitle says what the values are, and
the footer carries the byline, the source and any note.

```{r finished}
gg_map_chart <- ggplot(b) +
  geom_gla_sf(aes(fill = change)) +
  scale_fill_gla_b("diverging", name = NULL, steps = 3,
                   labels = label_gla_percent(scale = 1)) +
  gla_labs(
    title = "Employment has fallen in outer London since August 2025",
    subtitle = "Percentage change in payrolled employees, synthetic data",
    source = "HM Revenue and Customs, Pay As You Earn Real Time Information",
    note = "Estimates are based on where employees live",
    byline = "GLA City Intelligence"
  ) +
  theme_gla_map()
gg_map_chart
```

`gla_save("employment_map.png", gg_map_chart)` writes it at the house size.
For a dark surface, `gla_mode("dark")` before the chart recolours every
layer, as the [Get started](../articles/gglaplot2.html) page shows.

## Things that go wrong

- **The axes appear and the map sits in a box.** `theme_gla()` was used
  instead of `theme_gla_map()`. The map theme is the chart theme with the
  axes and gridlines taken away.
- **"Error: unexpected '+'".** A line in the chain begins with `+`. R ends
  the expression at the line break before it, so the `+` has to close the
  line above.
- **The legend goes to minus ten and nothing on the map is that low.** The
  limits were set wider than the data, or an old `breaks` outlived a data
  refresh. Drop them, or use `steps`.
- **An area is darker than its value.** It is beyond the limits and took
  the end step. Widen the limits or say so in the note.
- **Every rise is pale.** With few rises against large falls that is right,
  and `steps` gives the rises their own width. A smooth ramp,
  `scale_fill_gla_c("diverging")`, would stretch its darkest blue to the
  largest rise however small, which is why the stepped scale is the
  default for a map.
- **Values show as 0.05 rather than 5%.** The data is in fractions; use
  `label_gla_percent()` without `scale = 1`.
- **A borough is grey.** Its value is missing. Missing values take the
  `data-empty` token, and the note should say which areas have no data.
